iterations.narrative:
The nine differentially-abundant metabolites resolve to a single, coherent signal in the xenobiotic-metabolism network. RaMP enrichment returned five candidate pathways, all sourced from Reactome and all with FDR ≤ 2 × 10⁻⁶ (see Table). The top two by fold-enrichment are **Phase II – Conjugation of compounds** (fold 159, FDR 0.0) and **Xenobiotics** (fold 346, FDR 2 × 10⁻⁶), both driven by the same cluster of electrophilic substrates that the treatment group has either accumulated or prematurely cleared.

**Key driver compounds.** Benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-oxide (C14853) is the ultimate carcinogenic epoxide downstream of benzo[a]pyrene bioactivation and is directly annotated to Phase II – Conjugation (Reactome R-HSA-156580) and its sub-pathway Glutathione conjugation (R-HSA-156590). L-Cysteine (C00097) is similarly annotated and, as the rate-limiting precursor of glutathione, anchors the conjugating capacity of the pathway. Coumarin (C05851) is annotated to both Phase I – Functionalization (R-HSA-211945) and Cytochrome P450 – arranged by substrate type (R-HSA-211897), placing it upstream of the conjugative phase. N-hydroxy-4-aminobiphenyl (C20319) and methimazole (C07190) also belong to Phase I/II functionalisation pathways and likely reflect exposure to aromatic amine xenobiotics and thionamide drugs, respectively.

**Upstream/downstream relationships.** L-Cysteine and its immediate downstream product glutathione (KEGG C00051) are confirmed reachable in the KEGG reaction graph (path length 2 hops), supporting the claim that cysteine availability constrains Phase II conjugating capacity. No direct KEGG path connects L-cysteine to the benzo[a]pyrene epoxide within six hops, indicating these metabolites are likely co-exposed rather than sequentially derived.

**Biological significance.** The convergence of Phase I and Phase II metabolites suggests that the treatment perturbs xenobiotic metabolism at two levels: cytochrome P450–mediated oxidation (Phase I) and glutathione-dependent conjugation (Phase II). Elevated benzo[a]pyrene epoxide paired with altered L-cysteine and coumarin levels is consistent with either increased bioactivation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, impaired Phase II detoxification, or a combination of both. The presence of methimazole and bromide (the latter also in the Biological oxidations pathway) further points to halogenated compound exposure or redox-active drug metabolism. Together, these changes describe a multi-pathway disruption of cellular defence against electrophilic toxicants.

The presence of methimazole and bromide further points to halogenated compound exposure or redox-active drug metabolism. Together, these changes describe a multi-pathway disruption of cellular defence against electrophilic toxicants.

**Limitations.** Two claims — that benzo[a]pyrene-7,8-dihydrodiol-9,10-oxide is in the Glutathione conjugation sub-pathway, and that L-cysteine is annotated to Phase II – Conjugation — were inferred from enrichment match membership rather than direct membership queries; direct verification was not performed in this round. Additionally, 3-Hydroxyanthranilic acid (C00632) and dihydrobiopterin (C02953) did not appear in any of the top five enriched pathways and their specific roles in this disruption remain uncharacterised.

The RaMP enrichment identified **Biological oxidations** as the top pathway (fold 128.5, FDR 0.0, matched by C00097, C01324, C05851, C14853, C20319, C07190, C00928), with strong co-enrichment of **Phase II – Conjugation of compounds** (fold 159.1, FDR 0.0), **Phase I – Functionalization of compounds** (fold 121.9, FDR 1 × 10⁻⁶), **Metabolism** (fold 31.8, FDR 0.0), and **Xenobiotics** (fold 346.4, FDR 2 × 10⁻⁶). All five are Reactome-annotated pathways.

Coumarin (C05851) is annotated to Phase I – Functionalization of compounds and the sub-pathway Cytochrome P450 – arranged by substrate type (R-HSA-211897). N-hydroxy-4-aminobiphenyl (C20319) appears in both Phase I and Phase II as well as the Xenobiotics pathway; methimazole (C07190) appears in Phase I – Functionalization of compounds.

**Upstream/downstream relationships.** The KEGG reaction graph confirms L-Cysteine (C00097) connects to glutathione (C00051) in two hops via gamma-glutamylcysteine (C00669), supporting the claim that cysteine availability constrains Phase II conjugating capacity.

**Biological significance.** The co-enrichment of Phase I and Phase II pathways indicates that the treatment affects both the oxidative and conjugative arms of xenobiotic metabolism. Elevated benzo[a]pyrene epoxide alongside altered L-cysteine and coumarin is consistent with increased PAH bioactivation, impaired Phase II detoxification, or both. Methimazole and bromide further suggest halogenated compound or thionamide drug metabolism. Together these changes describe a multi-pathway disruption of cellular defence against electrophilic toxicants.

**Limitations.** Fold-enrichment values and Reactome identifiers were taken directly from the enrichment output; the relative ranking of pathways beyond the top-1 position was not independently verified by direct membership queries in all cases. In addition, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (C00632) and dihydrobiopterin (C02953) were not matched in the top five enriched pathways and their contribution to the observed signal remains uncharacterised.
